claims.text: The overall tribocorrosion degradation of high-entropy alloys is governed by the integrity of an in situ-formed oxide film.
Sintering temperature can tune the surface oxide-film quality of MgAlTiVFeCo.
Samples sintered at 850–950 °C have less continuous and less protective oxide films than a sample sintered at 1000 °C.
A MgAlTiVFeCo sample sintered at 1000 °C develops a dense, continuous, spinel-type oxide film.
The protective oxide film is enriched in Al and Fe.
High-temperature sintering promotes selective surface enrichment that generates the protective film.
The oxide film acts as a barrier to ion-driven corrosion.
The oxide film also acts as a barrier to mechanical wear and wear-induced material removal.
Mechanical sliding locally disrupts the oxide film.
Film disruption exposes fresh substrate that corrodes more rapidly.
The balance among film mechanical stability, regeneration or persistence, and wear-induced removal dictates coupled tribocorrosion degradation.
A high-temperature MgAlTiVFeCo sample has greater electrochemical film resistance and lower corrosion current density than lower-temperature samples in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
Under tribocorrosion, a sample with the dense oxide film will have less total material loss than the lower-temperature baseline.
If wear exceeds the film's protection or regeneration capacity, local corrosion damage will spike.
The mechanism should hold under moderate wear when film formation or stability is competitive with film removal.
The mechanism may fail under extreme loads that continuously remove the film or in environments that do not promote film reformation.
Lower-temperature baseline samples primarily undergo direct metal-solution corrosion with limited protective diffusion effects.
Comparing samples produced at different sintering temperatures isolates oxide-film integrity as the governing variable.
